title: Korach: Moses falls on his face (Numbers 16:4)
hook: attacked, Moses first falls on his face before answering
tomorrow: Korach: the man who went home

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah set Korach's quarrel beside Hillel and Shammai's, as the argument that doesn't last. Your line was not for heaven's sake. Did you catch yourself wanting the win more than the truth? Day four hundred fifty-three.

The message arrives at 11pm. It's sharp, it's public, and half of it is unfair. Thumbs start moving before the mind catches up. A reply sent in that moment can look very different by morning. In the Torah, Korach and two hundred and fifty leaders of the community gather against Moses and Aaron and accuse them, to their faces, of lifting themselves above everyone else. It's an attack on Moses' whole life's work. Everyone waits for his answer. Before he says a single word, he does something else.
screen: `A SHARP MESSAGE AT 11PM.` → `KORACH GATHERS AGAINST MOSES.` → `EVERYONE WAITS FOR HIS ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The verse is very short. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face." In Hebrew, that's va-yipol al panav. He drops to the ground, face down, in front of the crowd. The Torah doesn't explain why. The commentators fill the silence in different ways. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, reads it as distress: this was not the first time the people had turned on him, and Moses felt he had little left to say on their behalf. Others read it as prayer, a way of turning to God before turning to the people. Either way, notice the order. First he falls silent. Then he speaks. And when he does speak, he doesn't answer the insult. He says, in paraphrase, in the morning the Lord will show who is His. In the morning. He gives the night a chance. Rashi suggests Moses hoped that with a few hours, they might think again. Then Moses sends for two of the leading rebels, Dathan and Abiram, to talk. They refuse to come. But he tried. It's worth knowing that Moses falls on his face again and again in the book of Numbers: when the people despair after the scouts' report, and twice more during this very rebellion, pleading for the people's lives. It becomes a pattern when things fall apart. Not a weapon. A pause, with his face to the ground, before anything else.
screen: `HE FELL UPON HIS FACE.` · `DISTRESS, OR PRAYER, OR BOTH.` · `IN THE MORNING: TIME TO THINK AGAIN.` · `HIS FIRST MOVE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pause before replying to an attack. Settle, and lower your eyes, or close them. Bring to mind a time someone came at you with words: last week, or years ago. Notice how fast the answer wanted to come. Now, instead of answering, just let your head bow a little. Breathe in. Breathe out. Let the reply wait. See whether the silence gives you some room. If a better answer comes, keep it for later. Stay with your breath until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Korach. The rebellion that brought Moses to the ground before it brought him to his feet, falling on his face first, then answering.
Your line: fall silent first. Today, when a message stings, put the phone face down for one full breath before you write back. Day four hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: In traditional weekday prayer, a short section called tachanun is said with the head resting on the arm, and its traditional name, nefilat apayim, falling on the face, echoes the way Moses and Aaron fell on their faces in the wilderness.

pairs: the Lord will show who is His

myth: the Torah explains why Moses fell on his face
it doesn't. commentators read it as distress, as prayer, or both.
Moses falls on his face more than once in Numbers
after the spies' report, and more than once during Korach's rebellion.
Moses answered by defending his own record
he answered that in the morning the Lord would show who is His.

fork.setup: you're Moses. a crowd of leaders accuses you, publicly, of grabbing power. what's your first move?
options: answer every charge on the spot.
fall on your face, then speak.
walk away and say nothing at all.
fork.reveal: he fell on his face, then spoke, and even then he put the decision off until morning, giving everyone a night to think again.

original.note: Hebrew: and he fell on his face, Moses' first response to Korach (Numbers 16:4).

trapdoor: what you thought: Moses fainted, or gave up.
what it means: before answering an attack, he went silent and face down, then spoke, and bought time until morning.
what a scholar hears: Rashi links the fall to the people's repeated rebellions, and reads 'in the morning' as Moses giving the rebels a night to reconsider.

sources.quoted: And when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face.

notes: Numbers 16:4 in JPS 1917: 'And when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face.' Confirm wording.
Rashi on 16:4: this was already the fourth offense, and Moses felt his ability to intercede was weakened; on 16:5 'morning', Rashi says Moses hoped they might retract overnight. Confirm paraphrase.

Other occurrences of Moses (and Aaron) falling on their faces in Numbers: 14:5, 16:22, 17:10 (JPS numbering; 16:45 in KJV numbering), 20:6. Confirm the count implied ('twice more during this rebellion').
howItsDone links tachanun's posture (nefilat apayim) to Moses and Aaron; a Keeper may want to confirm or soften.
